claims.claim: Hong Kong should not tighten rent control on subdivided units beyond the current second-generation framework.
Stricter caps would deliver only modest tenant relief.
Stricter caps risk a slow contraction of the low-income housing stock.
About 110,000 households live in subdivided units.
SDU tenants pay a per-square-foot premium of 15 to 25 percent despite lower median rents.
SDU tenants are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households, and public housing waiters.
The average public housing wait has hovered around five and a half years.
For these households the SDU is a residual option, not a choice.
The long-run elasticity of SDU supply to controlled rent levels is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of SDU stock over five years.
Estimated SDU stock rose steadily from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025.
The 2021 ordinance is a second-generation control, which explains the stable stock.
First-generation controls show consistent contraction effects while second-generation controls show small or null effects.
Tightening would move policy closer to the first-generation end of the spectrum.
The per-square-foot premium is driven by scarcity and carving, not merely by the size of annual increases.
A tighter cap does not create space; it mainly redistributes existing marginal stock.
The durable fix is faster public housing queue turnover and more transitional supply.
Hong Kong should hold the second-generation framework, enforce it properly, and address the underlying shortage.

cites.sentence: About 110,000 households live in SDUs, and while median SDU rent is roughly 30 percent below mainstream flats, tenants pay a per-square-foot premium of 15 to 25 percent because space is priced at its most desperate margin [D1p1].
These tenants are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households and residents waiting for public housing, where the average wait has hovered around five and a half years [D1p2].
For these households the SDU is a residual option, not a choice [D1p2].
Standard theory predicts supply contraction under binding rent ceilings, though the elasticity is an empirical question [D6p1].

In marginal stock like SDUs, the long-run elasticity of supply to controlled rent levels is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48: a 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].
Estimated SDU stock rose from 100,800 units in 2019 to 107,300 in 2021, 109,800 in 2023 and 111,200 in 2025, with growth continuing through the ordinance [D2p1].
This is genuine evidence that moderate regulation did not trigger visible stock exit [D2p1].

First-generation controls show consistent contraction effects, while second-generation controls show small or null effects on stock — and the 2021 Hong Kong ordinance is second-generation, which explains the stable stock [D6p2].
Tightening would move policy closer to the first-generation end of the spectrum, where contraction effects are consistent [D6p2].
The current ordinance already caps increases within tenancies, and the stock data show it did not cause visible exit [D2p1][D6p2].
The current ordinance already caps increases within tenancies, and the stock data show it did not cause visible exit [D2p1][D6p2].
Stricter caps would push toward level controls with a known contraction record [D6p2], while the per-square-foot premium that actually burdens tenants [D1p1]
Stricter caps would push toward level controls with a known contraction record [D6p2], while the per-square-foot premium that actually burdens tenants [D1p1]
A tighter cap does not create space; it mainly redistributes the existing marginal stock and, at the margin, reduces the incentive to keep providing it [D6p1].

The premium persists because tenants have nowhere else to go while the public housing queue moves [D1p2]; the durable fix is faster turnover of that queue and more transitional supply, not a harder ceiling on a stock that is already growing slowly [D2p1].
